_comment: The per-service baseline for a PROVIDER's docker-compose manifest — the other half
of the code root. brokerimages.json beside this one pins the guest OS a provider
boots (trust-chain hop 3); it says nothing about the containers inside, because
mr_config_id commits to the app-compose the OPERATOR chose. This file is what says
which containers we accept.
WHAT IS RECORDED, AND AS OF WHEN. The twelve services below are cn-20's manifest —
provider 0x4870CbC4D07d6Ac2EE5aA865588e5985FE77a4E9, compose_hash
Each block was taken from that deployment's own `pcverify -provider -blocks` output
and its fingerprint checked back against the same output, so the recorded text is
the authenticated text and not a transcription of it.
RECORDING IS NOT APPROVAL, and this file is the wrong place to look for a claim that
the deployment is good. It answers one question — is this the deployment we recorded
— and the value of an answer is that it makes DRIFT visible: from here on, a service
added, removed, renamed, or changed in any way that changes what runs is a mismatch,
reported per service with the first differing line. Before there was an entry here,
an operator could have given the model server the container runtime's socket
overnight and nothing in the chain would have noticed.
WHAT IS KNOWINGLY ACCEPTED. The review (`pcverify -provider`,
client/evidence/composereview.go) reports ten blocking findings on this manifest, and
recording it here SILENCES NONE OF THEM — the review runs on every verification and
still says all ten. They are, with the per-service `note` fields below carrying the
detail: four images pinned by tag rather than digest (prometheus, grafana,
prometheus-node-exporter, dcgm-exporter), so for those four the compose hash commits
to a NAME whose contents the registry can republish after the measurement;
`privileged: true` on prometheus-node-exporter together with `/`, `/proc` and `/sys`
mounts; SYS_ADMIN on dcgm-exporter; and the container runtime's socket held by
0g-controller.
THE ONE ITEM THAT IS NOT JUSTIFIED is that last one, and it is an OPEN QUESTION
rather than an accepted risk: 0g-controller is OUR image, and it mounts
/var/run/docker.sock. A container holding that socket can start any container it
likes, privileged included, which makes the whole guest one trust domain and leaves
no per-service reasoning in this file worth much. It is recorded so that the mount
set cannot grow without a mismatch, NOT because anyone has established the
controller needs it. Until that is answered, this baseline must not be wired into
the sealing path as a refusal: enforcing a baseline whose central entry is
unexplained would convert an open question into a shipped decision.
IT RECORDS ONE PROVIDER, and that has a fleet consequence worth stating plainly: every
OTHER provider is now a mismatch, not a skipped check. That is the correct answer — we
have not reviewed their manifests — but it means this file cannot verify a fleet until
either the fleet converges on one manifest or the format grows a way to record several.
And convergence is not merely undecided, it is constrained by what a block contains:
0gm-sglang's recorded block carries `--model-path` and `--revision`, so a provider
serving a different model cannot match this baseline however correct its deployment is.
A baseline therefore describes one deployment shape, not a network — which is an
argument for recording several, not for pinning less, since dropping the model path
would leave the weights answering a sealed prompt unpinned.
Which way that goes is not decided here. What follows today: `pcverify -provider` exits 0 only
against a deployment recorded below, and 1 against any other, where before it exited 3
against all of them. Nothing in CI runs that command, so no automation changes behavior.
HOW AN ENTRY IS WRITTEN, and why it holds TEXT. Run `pcverify -provider <addr>
-blocks` against the deployment. It prints, per service, the canonical block and —
labelled `no-image:` — the same block with the image identity held out. Copy the
one the rule below needs into `block`, one array element per line. Do not
hand-format it: both sides are reduced by evidence.CanonicalizeServiceBlock at
comparison time, so what is stored need not match the emitter byte for byte, but a
transcription error is still a transcription error. Check the entry back with
`-app-baseline <candidate>` against the live provider before committing it.
Text rather than a digest, deliberately. A stored digest would bake the linked
gopkg.in/yaml.v3's formatting choices into this file, so a minor-version bump could
invalidate every entry at once and refuse every provider for a dependency upgrade.
Reducing both sides with one function at comparison time makes the library version
cancel out. And text is REVIEWABLE: a broker upgrade arrives as a legible diff
instead of a changed hash, which is the only way this file can be audited at all.
THE CANONICAL FORM IS NOT DEPLOYABLE YAML. Quoting is normalized away and the
image reference is replaced by `<image-held-out>`. It is a comparison form. Anything
that copies an entry into a compose file is misusing it.
THERE IS ONLY ONE IMAGE RULE, because the recorded block does the rest of the work.
`image` OMITTED — the default, and what nine of the twelve entries use. Copy the
`block` line from `-blocks` output. That text contains the image line, so it pins
the reference exactly as written: a digest, a bare tag, or no image at all,
whichever the deployment has. That is why the four tag-only images are recorded as
tag-only — a baseline answers 'is this the deployment we recorded', not 'is this
deployment good'.
"image": {"repository": "ghcr.io/..."} — any image in that repository, provided
it is pinned by digest. Copy the `no-image:` block instead, since the reference is
no longer pinned by the text. Used by the three entries that run 0G's own broker
image (0g-serving-provider-broker, 0g-serving-provider-event, 0g-controller), and
used ONLY there: without it a broker release would force a gateway release, three
entries at a time. It accepts an older official build — a risk taken knowingly, to
be closed by a denylist later. And it always requires a digest: without one the
reference names a tag whose contents the registry can republish after the
measurement, so 'any image in our repository' would mean 'whatever is there now'.
There is deliberately no `digest` or `reference` rule. An earlier draft had both, and
writing the tests showed they could only restate what the block's image line already
says — while making it possible to record a block naming one digest and a rule naming
another, which would fail with a message about the wrong thing. A redundancy that can
disagree with itself is not documentation. Both keys are REJECTED rather than
ignored, so an author reaching for them is told what the format does instead.
WHAT A MATCH REQUIRES (evidence.CheckCompose): every service listed here present
exactly once, every service in the manifest listed here, each block equal after
reduction, and each image satisfying its rule. A service the baseline does not
mention is a MISMATCH, not an omission — an unlisted container is unreviewed code
inside the same guest, and 'ignore what we did not think of' is how a baseline
becomes decoration.
AN EMPTY `services` LIST would mean NOT CONFIGURED: the comparison cannot run, warn
mode proceeds and says so, enforce refuses every provider and names the unfinished
configuration rather than blaming the enclave. It never means 'accept anything'.
Same contract osimages.json and brokerimages.json have, for the same reason.
Fields: `name` is the compose service key. `image` is the rule above. `block` is the
canonical text, one array element per line. `note` is the audit record for this
entry — why it is recorded as it is, and what the review says about it. It is
documentation: the comparison never reads it.

services.name: broker-ingress
note: dstack's own TLS terminator, pinned by digest. Holds /var/run/dstack.sock, which
the review reports to justify: a container with the guest-agent socket can derive
the app's keys and obtain quotes in the app's name. Accepted here because that is
precisely this service's job — the cert-binding quote the gateway verifies in
`pcverify -gateway` is the one this container obtains. The socket is why it must be
recorded, not why it should be removed.
block: - DOMAIN=${DOMAIN:?set DOMAIN — there is no default, so that a missing value cannot point this deployment at production}

services.name: 0gm-sglang
note: The model server, pinned by digest. Recording the block freezes --model-path and
--revision, which is the most load-bearing text in this entry: an unfrozen revision
means the weights answering a sealed prompt are the operator's later choice.
`ipc: host` is a review justify — shared memory is a channel nothing else in the
manifest names — and is accepted because the CVM is one guest and this is the
process the shared memory belongs to.

services.name: mysql
note: Pinned by digest. The root and user credentials are literals in the manifest, which
the review has no rule for and which is worth saying anyway: it is acceptable only
because the database is reachable on the compose network alone, never from outside
the guest. If a future manifest publishes a port for it, this note stops holding.

services.name: broker-config-init
note: Pinned by digest, and the reason to record it is the `command` text rather than the
image: this is the script that materializes config.yaml from BROKER_CONFIG and
substitutes PRIVATE_KEY into it. No image digest covers that script — only this
block does — so it is TCB the compose hash alone pins, and freezing it here is what
makes a change to how the broker's key is placed into the guest visible.
block: # First boot only. The controller's PUT /v1/config/core writes this same
# file and records the change in RTMR3, so rewriting it on every start
# would silently undo an operator change that is already on-chain — the
# same guard dstack's own boot script puts on docker-compose.yaml.
echo "BROKER_CONFIG is empty and no config exists yet" >&2
# Rename last, so a container killed mid-write leaves no half-file that
# the guard above would then accept as complete.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-broker
note: 0G's own broker image, recorded by repository so a broker release does not force a
gateway release. The image-held-out block is the one stored; note that the digest
also appears in IMAGE_DIGEST, which is why the hold-out erases the image IDENTITY
wherever it appears rather than just deleting the `image` key.
Two relative bind mounts (./logs/broker, ./logs/event) are review justifies: what a
relative bind exposes depends on the directory the deployment was brought up from,
which is not in the manifest. Accepted as log destinations; nothing reads back from
them.

services.name: 0g-serving-provider-event
note: Same image and the same repository rule as the broker service. Settles the
on-chain accounting, holds no host socket, and mounts ./logs/event — a relative
bind the review justifies for the reason given on the broker entry.

services.name: 0g-controller
note: THE OPEN ITEM IN THIS FILE. Same broker image, same repository rule, and it mounts
BOTH host sockets: /var/run/dstack.sock (review justify — it serves the attestation
proxy the other two reach over zg-tee, so this one is explicable) and
/var/run/docker.sock (review BLOCKING). The second has no justification recorded
because none has been established. A container with the runtime socket can start any
container it likes, privileged included; that it is our own image does not change
what the socket grants.
It is recorded rather than omitted so the mount set cannot grow silently, and the
review keeps reporting it blocking on every run. See this file's header: the
baseline must not become a refusal in the sealing path while this entry stands.
It also mounts ./logs/controller, a relative bind the review justifies for the reason
given on the broker entry.

services.name: prometheus-init
note: Pinned by digest. Like broker-config-init, recorded for its `command` rather than
its image — the default scrape config is generated here, and freezing it fixes what
the monitoring stack is pointed at.

services.name: prometheus
note: Review BLOCKING: prom/prometheus:v2.45.2 is pinned by tag, not digest. Recorded as
the deployment has it, which means this entry pins a NAME — the registry can
republish that tag after the measurement and the compose hash will not move. The
block still pins everything else, so the mount set and scrape target cannot change
silently, but the code behind the name can. This must become digest-pinned.

services.name: grafana
note: Review BLOCKING: grafana/grafana-oss:11.4.0 is pinned by tag — same consequence as
the prometheus entry above, and the same required change. Also two relative bind
mounts (./grafana/provisioning, ./grafana/dashboards): unlike the log binds
elsewhere, these are READ by the container, so what dashboards and datasources it
loads comes from a host directory the manifest does not describe.

services.name: prometheus-node-exporter
note: The worst entry in this file, and recorded anyway so it cannot get worse unnoticed.
FIVE review blockings: the image is pinned by tag; `privileged: true`; and `/`,
`/proc` and `/sys` each mounted from the host. Privileged inside a CVM means the
container holds every capability and sees every host device the guest has, which makes
the whole guest one trust domain — so no per-service reasoning in this file holds
beneath it, and recording the block does not repair that. What recording buys is that
the mount set and the command are frozen. Host metrics do not require this much: a
node exporter reading /proc and /sys read-only does not need `privileged` or `/`.

services.name: dcgm-exporter
note: Two review blockings: the image is pinned by tag, and cap_add grants SYS_ADMIN.
SYS_ADMIN is close to root on the guest and is the capability most container escapes
reach for. GPU profiling metrics are the usual reason an exporter is given it, which
is a reason and not a justification — the metrics are monitoring, and the capability
is inside the boundary that holds sealed prompts.
